item.title: No exit: Why Bangladesh's cities keep burning. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For the last fifteen years, buildings have been catching fire for the same reasons, with the same promises following each tragedy. If resilience truly starts at home, then home, in Bangladesh's cities, is precisely where it keeps failing.
Every October 13 , the world observes the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction. This year's theme, "Resilience starts at home," is meant to be read gently, as a call to prepare our households for disasters. In urban Bangladesh, it reads more like a warning.
A city that keeps reliving the same night
The roll call is long and familiar. From the Nimtoli chemical warehouse fire in 2010, which killed at least 124 people, to the Tazreen factory fire in 2012, the Bailey Road restaurant fire in 2024 and the Korail fire in 2025, Bangladesh's cities have repeatedly witnessed preventable loss of life and homes.
Across such incidents, well over 400 people have died. Almost none of the resulting court cases have reached a verdict.
The details differ, but the pattern does not: the conditions that allow a fire to become a disaster are often present long before the first flame.
The disaster is often built before the fire starts
Faulty electrical wiring and overloaded circuits are among the most common triggers. Gas cylinders used in homes, restaurants and vehicles can turn routine activities into deadly emergencies. Chemical warehouses and flammable stock are routinely stored in buildings never designed to contain them, turning a fire into an inferno within minutes.
Factories and high-rise commercial buildings with inadequate or locked emergency exits become death traps when smoke fills a corridor. Restaurants have proliferated on upper floors of buildings not designed for such use, sometimes obstructing escape routes. In informal settlements, tightly packed housing, exposed wiring and narrow lanes can allow a single spark to spread across an entire neighbourhood.
The problem, then, is not simply fire. Risk is built into the way buildings are designed, approved, occupied and maintained.
Rules on paper, risk in practice
Bangladesh is not short of regulation. The Bangladesh National Building Code, mandatory since 2006 and updated in 2020, sets out fire-resistant design, mandatory exits, hydrants, sprinklers and detection systems, and any building must secure fire safety clearance from the Fire Service and Civil Defence before RAJUK approves its design.
The gap is not in the law; it is in its application. A parliamentary disclosure put the share of Dhaka buildings violating the code at around 66 per cent. A RAJUK survey of over 200,000 structures found roughly two-thirds defective, risky or uninhabitable, while separate data found nine in ten surveyed buildings deviated from their approved designs. Too often, a design approved on paper is altered or repurposed in practice, without effective follow-up.
From certificates to inspections that bite
Closing this gap does not require new laws so much as the will to enforce existing ones. Building and fire approvals need to be digitised and linked, so a change of use or an expired licence is visible to regulators automatically rather than discovered after a tragedy.
Fire clearance should not be a one-time certificate issued at construction; it needs to be a recurring inspection, with real penalties, including sealing premises, for buildings that let it lapse. The Bangladesh Building Regulatory Authority envisaged under the BNBC 2020 should be operationalised with a clear mandate for consistent enforcement. RAJUK, city corporations and the Fire Service need enough trained inspectors to visit the hundreds of thousands of buildings under their jurisdiction. And court cases following major fires need to reach a verdict.
Six policy fixes we cannot keep postponing
Planners, engineers, lawyers and fire-safety experts have converged on broadly the same list of reforms after each tragedy; what has been missing is follow-through.
First , establish a dedicated Building Regulatory Authority to implement the Building Code consistently, instead of leaving it split across RAJUK, city corporations and the Fire Service with no single body accountable.
Second , harmoni z e the Fire Prevention and Extinction Act 2003 with the Building Code, so the two frameworks set the same standard.
Third , publish a tiered public registry of high- and moderate-risk buildings, so tenants and regulators know which structures need urgent attention before they burn.
Fourth , require every building to display an annually renewable occupancy and fire safety certificate at its entrance.
Fifth , make hospital, industrial and commercial fire protocols mandatory: functioning lifts, unlocked and clearly marked exits, refuge floors and regular evacuation drills.
Sixth , back all of this with real investment in the Fire Service's staffing and equipment, alongside a coordinated national occupational safety framework of the kind the International Labour Organization has urged Bangladesh to adopt since the Bailey Road incident.
Resilience starts at home, or it does not start at all
Every fire on this list was, in hindsight, foreseeable: a blocked exit, a warehouse in the wrong place, a licence never renewed. Resilience starting at home means exactly that literal thing here -- a safe electrical line, a clear staircase, a landlord who does not store chemicals beneath a family's bedroom.
Government agencies can write codes and NGOs can rebuild what fire destroys, but neither can retrofit safety into a building after the fact. Bangladesh's cities do not lack rules; they lack the follow-through to make those rules real, in every home, before the next spark catches.
Khondoker Golam Tawhid is the Programme Head of the Disaster Risk Management Programme at BRAC .

Fixing our banking sector. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Reports that the International Monetary Fund will likely press for strict, time-bound deadlines to fix weak banks and reduce the astronomical non-performing loans (NPLs) we have racked up should serve as a wake-up call for our leaders.
Despite dreams of self-sufficiency, the reality we must contend with is that, at present, our economic delegations are preparing to negotiate a fresh financial package with international lenders.
To that end, it is also abundantly clear that if we are to continue to receive the financial assistance our economy needs, Bangladesh can no longer afford half-measures in reforming what can safely be referred to as its crippled banking sector.
Decades of political patronage, reckless default cultures, and opaque loan write-offs have brought our financial architecture to the brink. As such, we simply no longer have the option to treat bank reform as an optional administrative exercise.
The rot in our financial system is neither hidden nor new. For years, massive amounts of liquidity have been siphoned off through fraud, insider lending, and willful defaults, leaving state-owned and private commercial banks saddled with staggering piles of debt.
It goes without saying that a banking sector choking on defaulted loans cannot be of help to the economy, thereby stunting our growth and deepening the broader fiscal crisis.
While no nation likes external pressure, we would do well to not view it as an infringement on sovereignty, but rather as a catalyst for accountability.
Financial stability is the backbone of national security and economic survival, and it is a shame that Bangladesh has not experienced it for some time now, if ever.
If setting strict deadlines is what is needed to cleanse our balance sheets and end the culture of loan default, then so be it. We must do what we can to restore public trust and build a modern, transparent banking system.

item.title: Controlling dengue requires a national strategy rooted in One Health. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Dengue in Bangladesh is no longer a temporary or seasonal health inconvenience; it has evolved into a persistent, multi-faceted public health crisis and a heavy burden on the national economy.
According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) dengue dashboard, over 107,000 individuals have been hospitalized, and more than 331 deaths have been officially documented as of October 15, 2026. With approximately 2,000 new patients admitted daily, the strain on the healthcare system is overwhelming.
Major tertiary hospitals in Dhaka and urban hubs are facing severe shortages of hospital beds and intensive care unit (ICU) capacities. Relatives face frantic scrambles for blood platelets, revealing the systemic fragility of urban medical infrastructure.
These alarming conditions highlight a critical truth: Reactive clinical management after people fall ill, paired with ad-hoc vector control drives, cannot control the transmission chain.
What Bangladesh urgently requires is a year-round, evidence-based preventive policy anchored in a coordinated national framework.
The uninterrupted spread of dengue is deeply intertwined with climate change, unplanned rapid urbanization, chronic waterlogging, and inadequate municipal waste management.
Global environmental and epidemiological research demonstrates that climate volatility, characterized by rising mean temperatures, erratic unseasonal precipitation, and elevated atmospheric humidity, dramatically accelerates the breeding cycles and vector efficiency of Aedes mosquitoes.
Under higher ambient temperatures, the duration required for the dengue virus to replicate inside the mosquito and reach its salivary glands, is significantly shortened. Consequently, an infected female Aedes mosquito becomes capable of transmitting the pathogen to human hosts much faster and more frequently within its lifespan.
Concurrently, urban environments proliferate with artificial micro-habitats. Construction sites, poorly designed drainage infrastructure, discarded single-use plastics, and poorly maintained rooftop gardens collect stagnant water, offering ideal breeding conditions.
Relying exclusively on hospital-centred curative care to address what is inherently an environmental and eco-climatic phenomenon is inherently flawed.
For decades, vector control efforts in Bangladesh have remained stubbornly reactive. Intervention plans are typically mobilized only after hospital admissions surge to crisis levels, taking the form of temporary fogging drives or hospital bed expansions.
Yet, such reactive measures fail to answer fundamental operational questions:
Indiscriminate fogging without routine entomological monitoring wastes municipal resources and damages urban ecosystems, killing beneficial non-target insects while accelerating insecticide resistance in Aedes vectors.
Transitioning from reactive fogging to sustainable vector management demands source reduction, routine larvicidal suppression, systematic waste removal, and targeted bio-control methods.
In this complex landscape, the 'One Health' framework offers the most viable path forward. One Health is an integrated, unifying approach that recognizes the intrinsic interdependence of human health, animal health, and the shared environment.
While dengue is not directly transmitted from animals to humans, it is a vector-borne viral disease reliant on the interaction between human hosts, viral pathogens, mosquito vectors, and ambient environmental conditions.
Applying One Health to dengue control means treating vector ecology, climatic dynamics, human mobility, and urban sanitation as a single interconnected ecosystem.
It breaks down traditional administrative silos, bringing together public health physicians, specialists, medical entomologists, environmental scientists, climate researchers, urban planners, and municipal engineers onto a unified operational platform.
The government recently formed a high-level special taskforce comprising representatives across various ministries and authorities to oversee mosquito-borne disease management, a commendable administrative step.
However, to translate policy into measurable health outcomes, this taskforce must move beyond administrative governance and actively embed the One Health framework into its operational core, with entomologists, climate specialists, and One Health practitioners needing to hold direct scientific advisory roles.
Crucially, Bangladesh needs a predictive national early warning and surveillance system that synthesizes real-time meteorological forecasts, rainfall patterns, vector density indices, larval mapping, and clinical hospitalization data.
Analyzing these spatial data streams will allow authorities to forecast outbreak clusters weeks before human cases spike, shifting intervention efforts from reactive crisis management to pre-emptive prevention.
Academic institutions and research centres must also be integrated into local intervention trials to evaluate the efficacy of eco-friendly larvicides and biological vector suppression tools tailored to micro-climatic zones.
Community participation remains vital to sustaining these interventions. Public awareness campaigns must empower citizens to inspect their surroundings, eliminate standing water, dispose of water-retaining trash, and neutralize mosquito breeding sites around homes.
However, civic responsibility must not serve as an excuse for institutional inaction. Local municipal authorities bear the primary obligation to ensure reliable solid waste collection, maintain open drainage canals, prevent waterlogging, and enforce environmental compliance across urban construction projects.
Controlling dengue demands a departure from fragmented, seasonal measures in favour of a long-term, science-driven, and accountable national strategy.
Clinical preparedness must be balanced with environmental management, integrated surveillance, and robust inter-ministerial coordination.
Ultimately, the success of national dengue control must not be measured by how many hospital beds are arranged to treat the sick, but by how many infections are prevented, how many vector breeding sites are permanently eliminated, and how many lives are protected.
Without a structural transition to a One Health paradigm, Bangladesh will remain trapped in a recurring cycle of preventable loss of life and severe economic strain year after year.
Professor Dr KBM Saiful Islam is the former Dean of the Faculty of Animal Science & Veterinary Medicine and former Chairman of the Department of Medicine & Public Health at Sher‑e‑Bangla Agricultural University. He previously served as a member of the National Coordination Committee of One Health Bangladesh.

Bangladesh is battling measles. It's a 'real warning' to other nations. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is battling to contain the world’s worst measles outbreak, a crisis exacerbated by weak data, inadequate outreach and vaccination gaps that experts say offers a warning to other nations about the deadly risk of falling immunisation rates.

Bangladesh, whose routine vaccination programme faltered in 2025, reported 202,000 suspected measles cases – 22,000 of them laboratory-confirmed – since the start of the outbreak in mid-March to October 9, the World Health Organisation said. That’s more suspected cases than any other country this year.

So far, 1,147 people have died of the highly contagious disease, with 94 per cent of reported deaths among children under five years old, the WHO said.

Bangladesh’s experience shows the challenge of containing an outbreak when vaccination coverage falls below 95pc, a level the WHO says is needed to prevent outbreaks. Bangladesh almost achieved that in recent years but in 2025 coverage dropped.

A Reuters review of WHO documents, alongside interviews with more than a dozen scientists, health workers and officials, shows Bangladesh was also hampered in its emergency response by data that left out millions of children, shortcomings in preparation and a failure to reach enough parents.

“This is a real warning to every country,” said Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser and professor at the School of Global Public Health at New York University.

Preventing an outbreak through vaccinations was easier, cheaper and safer than responding to an emergency, he said.

“The response will stop the outbreak eventually, but in the meantime, many will have had measles, and some will have died,” he said.

Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant on health affairs to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told Reuters in September the government was doing everything it could to end the outbreak. The government did not respond to further questions sent in October for this article.

‘They came only after i Buried my son’

In the northeast Sylhet region, one of the worst-hit areas in the nation of 178 million people, two-year-old Arman Hossain died unvaccinated in July, 24 hours after admission to hospital for treatment paid for by selling the family’s three-wheeled auto rickshaw. His unvaccinated four-year-old sister survived.

His father Amin Mia, 26, said no health workers came to their remote village in Sylhet to offer vaccinations in time. “They came only after I buried my son,” he said.

Measles usually kills two or three people in every 1,000 cases, the WHO says, but the disease can be more deadly in poorer nations because of factors such as malnutrition.

In the town of Chhatak, also in the Sylhet region, the daughter of 30-year-old carpenter Humayun Rashid died unvaccinated in June aged nine months. Labiba Akter could have received an inoculation in April when an emergency programme lowered the vaccination age to six months from nine.

“No health worker came to tell us,” her father said.

In a report published in July this year, WHO and UNICEF estimated first-dose coverage in 2025 had fallen to 90pc, while second-dose coverage was 86pc, several percentage points below the 95pc needed for herd immunity.

The report also raised questions about the quality of official data on vaccinations for measles and other diseases for the years 2023 to 2025.

It said preliminary figures sometimes showed numbers of those inoculated exceeded 100pc of those targeted, indicating mistakes in counting doses or target numbers.

Submitted by Areeb Ullah on Mon, 10/19/2026 - 12:59
Dhaka said it was not informed by Saudi Arabia that it had executed the pair arrested in Mecca for 'indecent acts'
Bangladeshi workers sitting outside an airport after flights to Saudi Arabia were cancelled following a series of Houthi attacks in October (AFP/Piyas Biswas)

Bangladesh is seeking answers on why Saudi Arabia executed two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca without telling Dhaka.

Last week, Saudi Arabia executed a male and a female Bangladeshi national after they were convicted of committing “indecent acts” inside a mosque.

Riyadh did not provide further details on the acts the two Bangladeshi nationals allegedly committed or whether they had legal representation in the Gulf kingdom, according to local media reports.

Reacting to the incident, Bangladesh’s minister for foreign affairs, Humaiun Kobir, told reporters that he was “very disappointed” by the lack of communication and that Dhaka was seeking an explanation on why they were executed and not informed beforehand about the execution.

“We have sought an explanation from our friendly bilateral partner to look into the matter and know why the gap in information sharing and exchanges happened here. We are in discussions," he told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday.

Earlier, the Bangladeshi foreign ministry said that it was waiting for a copy of the full verdict and the circumstances that led to the execution.

The official added that the two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh but did not indicate that they had planned to execute them.

Last week, Saudi Arabia’s Supreme Court overturned the death sentence of a Sri Lankan national after he allegedly insulted Islam and the Prophet Muhammad.

Sri Lanka’s Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra confirmed that Riyadh had overturned the death sentence of Anojan Sivarasa.

The 27-year-old remains imprisoned after he was sentenced to five years in prison and fined three million Saudi Riyals ($800,000).

The court handed down the sentence amid intense criticism of Riyadh's legal system.

Saudi Arabia relies on interpretations of Islamic law, alongside cybercrime and counterterror legislation, to target online expression under the guise of protecting "public morals".

This has resulted in a surge of decades-long prison terms for social media users and an increased use of capital punishment.

At least 175 people have been executed so far this year, the majority of whom are foreign nationals.

We cannot ignore our real wage crisis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We should be deeply concerned by the fact that inflation has outpaced wage growth for 56 consecutive months, as per reports from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS).
This streak of stagnant earnings falling behind soaring commodity prices can no longer be seen as a temporary metric of market friction and must be called what it is, and what it has been for some time - a full-blown livelihood crisis eroding the very fabric of our working and middle classes.
What must be recognized is the human toll behind these metrics, which is extremely stark. National survey data from BBS shows that to bridge the current shortfall, a staggering 47.42% of Bangladeshi households - and over 51% in rural areas - are needing to take on high-interest informal debt simply to put food on the table.
When citizens are forced to borrow money not to build assets, but to cover daily meals and basic utilities, we can conclude that the state’s socio-economic safety net has effectively failed. Given that this has been ongoing for almost five years now, this failure must be attributed to every single administration we have had during this time period.
In the absence of enforceable wage protections and automatic inflation-adjusted pay revisions, workers and employees alike are forced to absorb the full, brutal impact of macroeconomic shocks while corporate margins and profits remain shielded.
We cannot have a government that continues to remain a passive spectator to this erosion of basic purchasing power. Economic progress that enriches a privileged few while draining the savings of the working majority is morally indefensible, structurally unsustainable, and not the kind of progress any nation should be proud of.
The state must act now to restore real wages before our economic squeeze fractures our society beyond repair.

item.title: Why do foreign governments and lenders still want to invest in Bangladesh?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The IMF's October World Economic Outlook forecasts 3.2% growth for Bangladesh in FY27, down from 4.3% in April, with average inflation rising to 10.9%.
A week earlier, the World Bank cut its own forecast to 3.4% and said the weakness would persist through FY28, while it expects South Asia to grow at 6.9%.
If the IMF is right, this will be the slowest growth since FY1988-89, and place Bangladesh last among the seven South Asian economies in its table.
India is projected to grow at more than twice Bangladesh's rate. Sri Lanka, which defaulted on its external debt in 2022, is projected to grow faster than Bangladesh this year, as are Pakistan and Nepal. The medium-term outlook is weaker still, as the IMF projects Bangladesh's growth to fall to 2.2% in FY28 (Figure 1).
Yet over the same months, despite the grim forecasts for growth, the news from Dhaka has been of foreign governments and multilateral lenders showing strong interest in deepening their investments in Bangladesh.
The joint declaration of Bangladesh and China in June committed the two governments to modernize Mongla Port, develop a Chinese economic and industrial zone in Chittagong, and speed up the feasibility study for the Teesta project. In August, the Chinese ambassador said these projects could attract around 30 Chinese companies investing about $500 million.
Japan signed an Economic Partnership Agreement with Bangladesh in February and an emergency support loan for economic resilience and energy supply in June. Its plans now go further, as senior Japanese diplomats told The Hindu last week that Tokyo wants to build an industrial value chain around the JICA-financed deep-sea port at Matarbari, linking India's seven northeastern states, Nepal, Bhutan, and Myanmar to the Bay of Bengal. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is expected in Tokyo at the end of October to seek Japanese financing for a Matarbari industrial, port, and commercial hub for 2026-2031.
On October 13, the Dutch minister for foreign trade and development cooperation met the PM, who welcomed Dutch interest in the Teesta feasibility study. A senior US State Department adviser has said Bangladesh could soon become eligible for financing from the US international development finance corporation. South Korea expects its trade agreement with Bangladesh, still awaiting signature, to raise Korean investment.
The multilateral lenders show the same interest. Bangladesh is the largest borrower from the World Bank's International Development Association, with an exposure of $22.7bn as of March 2026. The ADB committed$2.685bn to Bangladesh in FY26. The relationship with the IMF is also intact.
The finance minister's statement on October 4 that he had cancelled the IMF program was read as an exit. In fact, the IMF confirmed in June that Bangladesh had applied for a new program, and in July, the finance minister said the two sides had agreed on its broad framework.
Little more than a week after his statement, the minister sought the support of the IMF and the World Bank in Bangkok. The government is leaving the program it inherited to negotiate new conditions. It is not leaving the fund.
Why would these governments and lenders want to invest in an economy that is not poised to perform?
My answer is that a market of more than 170 million people does not shrink when its growth rate does. That gives Bangladesh a bargaining position few countries with such a forecast have. The evidence from other countries supports four reasons.
Firstly , investors follow the size of a market more than its growth rate. In 2016, in the middle of a deep recession, Brazil still received about $78.9bn of foreign direct investment, nearly half of the inflows to Latin America.
The proposals for Bangladesh follow the same logic. The Invest Bangladesh pipeline is led by renewable energy and information technology, and the Chinese proposals include the Dhaka-Chittagong highway and waste-to-energy plants. These serve the domestic market.
By my own arithmetic, even 3.2% growth on an economy of about $470bn adds around $15bn of output in a year.
Secondly , governments compete for influence in large and well-placed countries. In 2015, Indonesia awarded the Jakarta-Bandung high-speed rail to China over Japan after China agreed to build it without an Indonesian government guarantee, while Japan had offered a loan at 0.1% interest.
Bangladesh sits in the same contest, as China, Japan, the Netherlands, and the United States all seek a role in its ports, rivers, and energy.
China and the Netherlands have both offered support on the Teesta feasibility study. Japan's answer is Matarbari, and its diplomats cite the Southern Economic Corridor linking Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam as the model.
Thirdly , supply chains are moving out of China. Vietnam drew a record $25.35bn in foreign direct investment in 2024 as manufacturers diversified, helped by its trade agreements and lower labour costs.
The agreement with Japan, China's zero-tariff treatment of Bangladeshi goods, and the planned agreement with South Korea give Bangladesh a similar platform.
Fourthly , multilateral lenders do not walk away from large borrowers. In 2024, Egypt secured an IMF program of $8 billion, a World Bank package of $6 billion and EU support of €7.4bn. In Nigeria, where I also work, the World Bank approved about $9.35bn between June 2023 and May 2026, after the government removed the petrol subsidy and unified the exchange rate. In my reading, the financing in both countries was tied to reform.
However, most of this interest is still a promise, not an investment.
Ashik Chowdhury, who now chairs Invest Bangladesh, said in June that the Chinese company’s proposals had not been verified. Of the $1.3bn pipeline his agency reported in September, only a little over $400m had reached the decision or implementation stage.
UNCTAD puts total foreign direct investment into Bangladesh in 2025 at $1.8bn, and the World Bank's own commitment fell to $820m in FY26, its lowest. Interest lapses if the government does not convert it.
To secure these investments, the Ministry of Finance should conclude the new IMF program quickly, as finance ministry officials themselves describe an active program as a seal of approval that unlocks other financing.
In return, the government should accept the IMF’s conditions on raising tax revenue. Bangladesh collects only 8.3% of GDP in tax, among the lowest ratios in the world. The IMF mission discussed measures to raise that ratio as early as July, and no lender will drop the condition.
Each G2G partnership also needs a single owner in government and a published timetable, as the published accounts of the declaration with China give no cost or date for Mongla, Chittagong, or Teesta.
Invest Bangladesh should publish a quarterly tracker of every proposal and its stage. The government should also hold to the five-year tax outlook it presented to Chinese investors.
Size is the reason an economy like Bangladesh always has room to turn around. The governments and lenders now showing interest are betting on the market, not on this year's growth rate.
However, the turnaround will not happen unless the government removes the constraints the World Bank has named: Gas and electricity shortages that disrupt industry, non-performing loans that reached 33.2% in June, and weak revenue collection.
The Matarbari plan also depends on relations with India, as the Maitri Bridge over the Feni river, the link to Tripura, is not operating.
The government will keep its bargaining position only if it turns this interest into signed investment before the investors look elsewhere.
Md Rubaiyath Sarwar is Managing Director of Innovision Consulting and Trustee at Panam Institute, an Economic Think-Tank .

Off

Sameen Ud Din has lived at the same address in Old Delhi for years. He voted in the 2025 Delhi elections. But when the draft voter list for the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, was published this time around, his name was missing.

“It is an irony not to find my name in the SIR list. I did not receive any notice from the Election Commission of India [ECI] when my name was deleted,” Din, a 44-year-old businessman from the Nizam Ud Din area of Old Delhi, told Middle East Eye.

“I am now being asked to fill out Form 6, an application to register as a new voter, which is clearly a false declaration and carries penal consequences,” he added.

Din said he did not know what would happen next and felt pressured to submit the form. India's next general election is in 2029.

But Din is not alone. Muslims in different parts of India have reported similar problems, with countless people finding their names missing from the draft voter lists.

Approximately 133 million names had been flagged for removal from the voter list.

Critics say many eligible voters have been removed, with Muslims and Dalits – Dalits occupy the lowest rung in Hinduism’s caste system – among those mostly affected. 

An investigation from The Wire shows that in West Bengal, out of 2.75 million on the published list of removals, approximately 1.8 million were Muslims - or around 70 percent of the total published "ineligible to vote" list. Muslims make up just 25 percent of that state's electorate.

In some districts, according to The Wire, removals of Muslims made up over 90 percent of the total published removals.

This disparity has also brought protesters onto the streets of New Delhi. At one mid-October protest, India's Congress Party estimated that 250,000 people were present, while tens of thousands have been protesting across the country.

Protests suppressed

The Cockroach Janta Party, or CJP, called for demonstrations against the SIR under the slogan “Lehra Do Tiranga” or “Wave the Tricolour”. Protesters carrying national flags gathered at Connaught Place before moving towards Dilli Haat and other parts of central Delhi.

“Gyanesh Kumar, resign”, “Down with Delhi Police”, and “Whenever Modi is scared, he sends the police to the front” were among the other slogans protesters shouted.

'Our demand is clear: roll back the SIR because it is a state tool to change the country’s voting demographics'

- Vishnu, protester

The CJP began in May 2026 as a satirical online movement founded by digital strategist Abhijeet Dipke.

At the time, the movement was demanding the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, a senior leader of the Bharatiya Janata Party or BJP, and the education minister in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s cabinet. The protest came after the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET), one of the world’s largest medical entrance exams, was leaked; it determines admissions into five-year undergraduate medical courses in India.

It has since developed into a street protest movement.

Today protesters now want the government to stop the SIR and demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Figures cited by the ruling BJP show that about 130 million names were dropped from draft voter lists during the revision of the list. The ECI says the deletions are meant to clean up the rolls by removing the names of dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.

The protests against these actions took place despite a ban imposed by the BJP-led Delhi government on gatherings of four or more people in some areas. 

The restrictions came after Delhi Police removed Jantar Mantar, an 18th-century observatory and a long-time protest site, from its list of approved protest locations on 12 October. Police named Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi as alternative locations.

“We are out to protest to protect democracy. There is no violence going on, but the police are still detaining people. It is illegal. These detentions are a symbol of a fascist state, and this has been happening in India for a long time,” a protester who gave only his first name, Vishnu, told MEE.

He was speaking from a private vehicle hired by Delhi Police to transport detained protesters.

“Our demand is clear: roll back the SIR because it is a state tool to change the country’s voting demographics. They have done it successfully in many places, and we want people to join us and fight this fascist government with us,” he added.

Police detained several CJP leaders and protesters during the demonstrations, including Dipke and All India Students Association president, Neha Bora.

Bora was released on Saturday morning. Dipke appeared before a Special Executive Magistrate court and was released after signing a bond, according to reports. Delhi Police registered at least two cases over the march for violating prohibitory orders.

‘Deleted votes are those of Muslims’ 

On 23 September, The Indian Express published an investigation into alleged irregularities at the Election Commission. The report said the ECI had bypassed legal requirements, raised concerns over the SIR and centralised the voter database.

It also reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times in 10 months to decisions and orders issued without their knowledge, approval or consultation. Their concerns included the addition and deletion of voters, changes to Form 6, access to the electoral database, and the commission’s technology systems.

The ECI rejected claims of an internal rift. It said the notes were suggestions and that every decision taken in the past year, including those related to the SIR, was unanimous. 

Where do Muslim youths fit in India's 'Cockroach' protests?
Read More »

For SIR critics, however, the concern goes beyond the Election Commission's functioning. They say the revisions could determine who can vote and, in turn, affect India’s political landscape. 

Ajay Gudavarthy, an associate professor at the Centre for Political Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi, said available data on voter deletions suggested that Muslims made up a large share of those removed from the rolls. 

He said he believed the deletions were part of a wider political strategy targeting Muslims and Dalits while building support among Other Backward Class, or OBCs, and upper castes. OBC is an official term employed by the government of India and is an umbrella classification for communities that are deprived or disadvantaged, whether economically, socially or in terms of education. 

“An overwhelming majority of the deleted votes are those of Muslims. This is one reason there is no mass outrage against the SIR. The BJP’s larger design is not only to delete Muslim votes but also to socially polarise people on the basis of these deletions,” Gudavarthy told MEE.

“Alongside Muslims, Dalit votes are also being deleted in order to achieve a reverse consolidation of OBCs and the upper castes,” he added.

The experience of Sayed Rashad Ikmal’s family in Odisha shows how the deletion of names can affect voters at the local level.

Ikmal, a resident of Sungra village in Cuttack district, said the names of his aunt and her husband were missing from the draft SIR voter list, even though his uncle had worked in the finance department of Indian Railways.

“The omission came as a shock to the family, which, like several others in the village, worried about being left off the voter rolls,” Ikmal told MEE.

The family approached the booth-level officer and found that a Form 7 application had been filed with the ECI seeking the deletion of their names. Form 7 is used to object to the inclusion of a name or request the removal of an existing name from the voter roll.

The family later approached the Block Development Officer [BDO], who cancelled the request and restored both names to the SIR list, Ikmal told MEE.

He said the BDO's role was important because local officials could prevent people from being wrongly removed from voter lists. 

India's 'Cockroach Party' takes aim at Narendra Modi's government after national exam debacle
Read More »

“If the BDO does his job honestly, wrongful additions to or deletions from the voter rolls can be stopped, whatever happens at the higher level,” he said.

The residents of Sungra and nearby villages, Ikmal said, had begun to feel that Muslims were being targeted in Odisha. He said these concerns had grown alongside the spread of the “Go to Bangladesh” narrative among people linked to Hindu right-wing groups.

“I describe the threat of being sent to Bangladesh as one of the most intimidating narratives directed at Muslims,” Ikmal said, referring to political claims about Bangladeshi infiltration into Assam and West Bengal.

“The narrative had been used to divide voters ahead of state elections in both states and to build support for the BJP,” he added.

For Gudavarthy, the issue points to a larger question about the strength of India’s democratic institutions.

“The system needs to be made accountable only through mass protests and institutional decentralisation,” he said. “It is a lesson for Indian democracy that institutions can be so easily subverted when there is executive overreach,” he added.

item.title: Aurangzeb rules out consumption-led growth, says tariff reforms will continue. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb has ruled out pursuing liquidity-fuelled, consumption-led economic growth, saying Pakistan must prioritise sustainable, export-led expansion and continue with tariff reforms to improve the competitiveness of its industries.

Speaking at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (Lums) on Saturday, Aurangzeb said Pakistan could not afford to repeat the cycle of import-dependent growth that had previously led to balance-of-payments problems and forced the country to seek support from lenders of last resort.

He said the government was committed to continuing tariff reforms, primarily to reduce the cost of raw materials and intermediate goods for exporters, despite concerns over the timing of the measures.

“We are very clear: no matter how much pressure there is, we are not going to go for liquidity-fuelled, consumption-led growth,” he said, adding that Pakistan needed to avoid another cycle in which a temporary acceleration in economic activity was followed by a balance-of-payments crisis.

Aurangzeb said the government had attempted to provide a direction towards export-led growth in the latest budget through measures including the elimination of super taxes, reductions in tax slabs and financing for exporters at 4.5 per cent.

On tariff reforms, he said the government had protected domestic industries for too long without sunset clauses and that the existing approach could not continue indefinitely.

“We are in year two of the tariff reform, and we are going to continue with that; there is no turning back,” he said.

The finance minister also stressed that economic growth needed to generate employment, pointing to the contrast between Pakistan’s growth trajectory and that of its neighbour, where growth of 7 to 8pc, he argued, had not translated into sufficient job creation.

“That’s why you see people there where they are,” he said, emphasising that the sectors driving growth must also address unemployment.

Global outlook remains uncertain

Reflecting on discussions at international forums in New York, London and Bangkok ahead of the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Aurangzeb said the global economy had remained resilient but faced an uncertain and worrying outlook.

He identified growing differences in economic fortunes between oil-exporting and oil-importing countries, as well as economies benefiting from artificial intelligence, as key themes in discussions on global growth.

Energy shocks and the El Nino weather phenomenon had featured prominently in discussions, he said, warning that their effects were intensifying and contributing to food-security concerns in some parts of the world.

He also highlighted high debt levels, limited fiscal space in some economies and the growing importance of digital infrastructure and labour-market preparedness for artificial intelligence.

As trade fragmentation and geopolitical polarisation intensified, regional corridors and regional blocs were emerging as significant opportunities, he said, adding that these developments could be particularly important for Pakistan.

Twin deficits narrow

The finance czar said Pakistan had made significant progress in reducing its fiscal and external imbalances, with the combined twin deficits falling from 12.5pc of gross domestic product (GDP) to 2.6pc by the end of the last fiscal year.

He said the fiscal deficit had dropped to a 22-year low, while the country had recorded primary surpluses for three consecutive years. The current account deficit narrowed to around 0.1pc of GDP, supported by remittances and IT exports.

Aurangzeb said IT export services had risen from less than $1 billion to $4.6bn and were projected to reach $5.5bn in the current fiscal year. Foreign exchange reserves had improved to over three months of import cover, compared with two weeks during the crisis.

Citing three credit-rating upgrades since April last year, he said a recent Panda bond had attracted an order book twice its size, reflecting investor confidence beyond Pakistan’s current IMF programme, due to end in October next year.

Conflict puts pressure on energy security

He further said that Pakistan had managed immediate energy-supply challenges amid the continuing Middle East conflict, with supplies secured through November and arrangements for winter underway.

He said the government had shifted from blanket subsidies to targeted support, citing the high cost of universal subsidies.

Assuming an average household size of four to five people, the programme had reached an estimated 40 million to 50 million people, he said, adding that energy and gas supplies remained areas requiring attention.

Debt management and access to finance

The minister maintained that government borrowing had placed a disproportionate burden on the banking sector, but domestic debt-management operations had helped reduce debt-servicing costs to Rs6.9 trillion against a budgeted Rs8.2tr in the last fiscal year.

He said external debt payments had declined from $26.5 billion last year to $21.5bn in the current fiscal year and were expected to fall further. New external borrowing was largely aimed at replacing existing obligations, rather than increasing the debt burden.

Aurangzeb also highlighted pension reforms, saying new entrants to the civil bureaucracy had shifted from defined-benefit to defined-contribution schemes, while discussions with the armed forces were ongoing.

Population, investment and inclusive growth

The finance minister said the government has identified climate change and population growth as major challenges for Pakistan, urging measures to reduce the country’s 2.55pc population growth rate.

He cited Bangladesh, Indonesia and Iran as examples, saying all three had reduced their population growth rates to below 1pc over a decade. He stressed women’s education, workforce participation and engagement with religious scholars as key measures.

Aurangzeb said restoring investor confidence required macroeconomic stability and the clearance of around $4 billion in outstanding dividend and profit repatriation obligations.

He also highlighted improving domestic investment, citing 11 initial public offerings last year — a 20-year high — and five in the current year.

The finance minister said harmonising federal and provincial regulatory frameworks was essential to attract investment, as businesses often faced differing requirements at both levels. He stressed that reforms in taxation, energy and financing were necessary to sustain growth, improve export competitiveness and create jobs.

item.title: The 18 months that changed Bangladesh. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In August 2024, the streets of Dhaka smelled of smoke and uncertainty. Autorickshaws fell silent. Shopkeepers pulled down shutters early. The old order had collapsed, and in its place stepped an 84-year-old Nobel laureate who promised to shepherd Bangladesh toward democracy.
Eighteen months later, in February 2026, those same streets erupted in celebration. The BNP won a sweeping victory, and Tarique Rahman was sworn in as prime minister. The transition felt complete, a return to the democratic fold after an unelected interregnum.
But as we mark eight months of the new government, a question lingers: What exactly happened during those 18 months?
The Yunus-led interim government departed, handing over power with farewell speeches about sovereignty and dignity. Yet they left behind a trail of shadowy decisions and unanswered questions.
They governed without an electoral mandate but with immense moral authority, born of a mass uprising. That authority came with an obligation: To be more transparent than any elected government, not less.
We have crossed the bridge back to democracy. But the bridge itself was built with materials that now demand inspection. It is time to light a torch and walk back into that tunnel.
The ledger of lost lives
The most damning indictment of the interim government’s priorities is written in the bodies of dead children.
Bangladesh is now in the grip of the world’s worst measles outbreak. Starting mid-March, over 200,000 have been hospitalized across the country, with the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak being 1,242 as of today. 94% of them were children under five.
In Sylhet, Amin Mia sold the family’s autorickshaw to pay for hospital treatment for his two-year-old son, Arman. The boy died unvaccinated in July. “They came only after I buried my son,” Mia said.
In Chhatak, Humayun Rashid’s nine-month-old daughter Labiba died in June. She was eligible for vaccination in April, when the emergency program lowered the age threshold to six months. “No health worker came to tell us,” her father said.
The outbreak was preventable. In September 2025, the interim government stopped purchasing vaccines through UNICEF -- a reliable system that had worked for years -- and switched to an open tender system, a move widely suspected to be a precursor to privatizing vaccine procurement.
The tender stalled. Vaccine stock depleted. A planned nationwide campaign was cancelled. By 2025, first-dose coverage had fallen to 90% and second-dose to 86%, both below the 95% threshold needed for herd immunity.
The current government reinstated Unicef procurement and launched an emergency campaign in April. But the response has been incomplete.
A Reuters investigation found that the campaign’s target list excluded four million children in the eligible age group. By August, the proportion of confirmed cases who were unvaccinated had actually risen, from 82% to 85%.
The children who died were failed twice: First by the procurement decision, then by the response to its consequences.
The architecture of opacity
When Yunus addressed the nation in those first days, he spoke of transparency. He promised that all advisers would disclose their assets. That promise gathered dust like an abandoned building.
Instead, what emerged was a pattern of decisions that benefited entities intimately connected to the chief adviser himself.
Within two months of Yunus taking office, the National Board of Revenue granted Grameen Bank a five-year income tax exemption until 2029, reversing a 2020 decision. Based on previous records, the bank used to pay around Tk 200 crore annually in taxes, meaning the total revenue loss to the government over five years is estimated to exceed Tk 1,000 crore.
Grameen University, established by Yunus, received approval within three months of applying, while applications from at least 22 other private universities remained pending for years.
Then came the legal reckoning. In September 2026, the High Court ordered Grameen Kalyan, founded by Yunus, to pay Tk 666 crore in outstanding taxes for 2012 through 2017.
The court rejected the organization’s writ petitions, paving the way for the NBR to collect. Jurist Shahdeen Malik said there would be “a certain perception” about the facilities received and that “conflict of interest is another dimension which should have been considered more seriously.”
Transparency International Bangladesh warned that reforms initiated by the interim government had “largely failed” to ensure institutional independence and accountability. TIB concluded that resistance from entrenched interests had derailed much of the interim government’s reform agenda.
The politics of rewriting the past
Perhaps nothing reveals the interim government’s political project more clearly than its enabling of historical erasure.
On February 5, 2025, crowds responding to social media calls for a “bulldozer procession” systematically dismantled the Bangabandhu Memorial Museum at Dhanmondi 32, the historic residence of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.
The crowd first vandalized and set fire to the museum around 8:30 pm, and by 11:10 pm, an excavator had been brought to the site. Police had deployed additional forces but “did not create any major obstacles to those moving to the museum in processions.”
The interim government issued a statement calling the events “unexpected and unintended.” Transparency International Bangladesh criticized the government’s “alarming nonchalance.”
A case petition was filed against 27 individuals including Yunus and former law adviser Asif Nazrul. The court dismissed it for “lack of grounds.” No arrests have been made. The accused remain free.
The first demolition occurred under the interim government. The precedent was set in February 2025, when an unelected government with a moral mandate to uphold justice stood by while a national museum was demolished by mobs.
The geopolitical gamble
In his farewell address, Yunus declared that Bangladesh had restored its “sovereignty, national interest, and dignity” in foreign policy. But what did this rhetorical sovereignty actually mean in practice?
On February 9, 2026, just three days before the general election, the interim government signed the US-Bangladesh Agreement on Reciprocal Trade. An analysis of the 32-page agreement found a sharp imbalance in its language: “Bangladesh shall” appears 131 times, while “US shall” appears just six times.
The agreement requires Bangladesh to align with US sanctions regimes, accept US regulatory standards for agricultural products, relax foreign ownership limits in key sectors, and accede to a long list of international intellectual property treaties within specified timelines.
It also embeds binding procurement commitments: 14 Boeing aircraft, approximately $15 billion in American LNG offtake, and 700,000 metric tons of US wheat annually.
The agreement was signed by a government with no electoral mandate, three days before the people it governed were given the chance to choose their own representatives. By what authority did an unelected administration bind the nation to these terms?
The republic’s right to know
An unelected government has no built-in accountability mechanisms. No parliament to answer to. No opposition to monitor its actions. That is precisely why the Yunus government bore a special obligation, a moral obligation, to be more transparent than any elected government could be expected to be.
Yet over 18 months, serious allegations of corruption and abuse of power were raised against several advisers. And they were met with little visible response.
TIB’s Corruption Perceptions Index for 2025 showed Bangladesh’s score rising by only one point to 24, the second-lowest in 14 years. TIB stated that the interim government “failed to take effective and exemplary measures against corruption” and that money laundering had not stopped.
This is not a call for prosecution. It is a call for disclosure. Publish the full text and annexes of the trade agreement. Publish the vaccine procurement timeline. Publish the tax exemption list. Publish the chain of command on Dhanmondi 32.
If the documents show nothing, the interim government is vindicated. If they show something, the public learns what was done in its name. Disclosure does not require a tribunal. It requires a government willing to release paper.
The interim government is gone. But its decisions are not. The trade agreement runs for years. The tax exemptions run to 2029. The measles outbreak is ongoing. The demolition is permanent.
The silence of the current government on these matters is itself part of the story. Why has the new government not repealed the trade agreement, investigated the procurement, or pursued the Dhanmondi 32 case?
The audit demand is not directed only at Yunus. It is directed at whoever currently holds the power to disclose and chooses not to.
We call for a parliamentary commission to review every foreign agreement signed during this period. We call for the full list of tax exemptions received by Yunus and connected institutions to be made public. We call for a full accounting of the vaccine procurement decisions that led to the measles outbreak. The children who died deserve nothing less. And we call for an investigation into the demolition of Dhanmondi 32: Who gave the order, and why no one was held accountable.
These investigations are not intended to defame Yunus or his advisers. They are required in the interest of the nation itself. Examining this interim administration’s powers, responsibilities, and shortcomings can help establish a framework for future caretaker governments. We must assess where mistakes were made or limits exceeded so that similar problems can be avoided in the future.
The citizens of Bangladesh, who braved bullets in July 2024, who demanded democracy, who sacrificed for a better future, deserve nothing less.
They own this republic. They have a right to know what was done in their name during those 18 months when decisions were made in the dark.
The sun has risen on a new government. But shadows remain. Let us chase them out, together.
Zakir Kibria is a Bangladeshi writer, policy analyst and entrepreneur based in Kathmandu, Nepal. His email address is zakir.kibria@gmail.com . Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: Can Bangladesh’s cyber police outrun its institutions?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A police officer watching a crowded street sees only what is in front of them. A cyber police officer can potentially see patterns across thousands of phones, accounts, images, and videos.
Bangladesh is now developing the capacity to do much more of that.
On October 1, the country launched its new Cyber Police Unit with an approved structure of 4,592 posts. The unit is tasked with investigating cyber and financial crimes, analyzing digital evidence, monitoring social media and the dark web, and using AI-assisted video analytics and facial identification. Cyber desks are planned for police stations, alongside a 24/7 cyber support centre.
The case for expanding cyber policing is straightforward. Criminal activity increasingly leaves a digital trail, and police need the expertise and technology to follow it.
But a more capable cyber police force also raises a less comfortable question: Can the institutions governing these new powers develop as quickly as the powers themselves?
Digital policing is not merely about catching criminals more efficiently. It also concerns who can access information, how it is interpreted, and what happens when the state gets it wrong.
Bangladesh is not starting from scratch. The Criminal Investigation Department (CID) has operated its Cyber Police Centre since 2017 to deal with cybercrime and related digital investigations.
Since 2020, the Bangladesh Police’s Police Cyber Support for Women (PCSW) has provided legal and technological assistance to women facing cybercrime, including counselling and referrals to police stations, specialised units and victim-support centres. Broader reporting channels include police stations and the national emergency service, 999.
The challenge is not just creating more places for victims to report. It is making these channels work together.
A woman reporting image-based abuse, for example, should not have to know whether her case belongs with a local police station, a new cyber desk, the Cyber Police Centre, PCSW, or another specialized unit.
Her case should reach the right expertise without requiring her to navigate the bureaucracy herself.
That becomes more important as the new unit expands. The 4,592 figure represents approved posts, not a fully staffed force. Existing police personnel will initially fill positions before additional recruitment. The cyber desks and 24/7 support centre will also have to move from organisational plans to functioning services.
But the harder questions begin once the police have the data.
Who can access sensitive digital evidence? How long should it be retained? When can it be shared with another agency? How should investigators document the use of AI-assisted systems? And what happens when an automated identification or analysis is wrong?
A mistaken police conclusion about a digital identity, image, or online interaction can affect an investigation, a person’s reputation, or their freedom. As analytical tools become more powerful, scrutiny of their conclusions becomes more important.
Bangladesh’s Personal Data Protection Act 2026 establishes a broader framework for protecting personal data while allowing processing without consent where necessary for the prevention, detection, inquiry, investigation or prosecution of offences.
That is important for law enforcement. But a general data-protection framework cannot by itself determine how every police database, forensic system or AI-assisted tool should be operated.
Accountability matters especially because Bangladesh’s recent police oversight framework remains unsettled.
The 2025 Police Commission Ordinance included a mechanism for citizen complaints, but that framework is no longer in effect.
This creates a sequencing problem. It is relatively easy to acquire technology and create new police posts. It is harder to build durable institutions capable of scrutinizing how that technology is used.
Once databases, analytical systems, and specialized investigative practices become embedded, changing the rules around them becomes more difficult.
Bangladesh should build safeguards alongside capability. The new Cyber Police Unit should connect with existing victim-support and referral services rather than set up another isolated reporting channel.
Police should have clear operational rules governing access to, retention, and sharing of digital evidence, as well as procedures for documenting and challenging consequential errors in automated analysis. Citizens also need credible avenues to question misuse of digital investigative powers.
The future of cyber policing will not be determined only by what police can see. It will be determined by what they are allowed to do with what they see, and whether citizens have meaningful ways to challenge them when they get it wrong.
Ashfaq Ferdous is an academic at Southeast University, Bangladesh, and a former Assistant Superintendent of Police with Bangladesh Police.

item.title: How exposed is Bangladesh to a prolonged Saudi crisis?. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is unlikely to see an immediate fall in remittances from Saudi Arabia even as Houthi attacks on the kingdom intensified from early October, but a slowdown in new migration could weigh on inflows in the years ahead.

Following the attacks, migration to Saudi Arabia, the largest destination for Bangladeshi workers, has already been disrupted. As of Sunday, 144 direct and transit flights had been affected by prolonged flight restrictions at Saudi airports, disrupting the travel plans of around 22,000 passengers.

But economists and manpower experts say remittance inflows are unlikely to be hit immediately because newly arrived migrant workers typically take about a year to start sending significant amounts of money home.

According to them, the longer-term impact will depend on the duration of the crisis, the performance of the Saudi economy and demand for labour, particularly in construction.

A prolonged crisis that damages the Saudi economy could slow job creation and reduce workers’ incomes. But the outcome is not necessarily negative for the kingdom’s economy.

If Houthi missile and drone attacks continue without damaging oilfields and refineries, higher global oil prices could boost Saudi revenues, potentially supporting investment and demand for foreign workers, according to Zahid Hussain, a former lead economist at the World Bank’s Dhaka office.

“But everything is uncertain so far,” he commented.

Remittances are a major source of foreign currency for Bangladesh, accounting for around 7.5 per cent of gross domestic product, according to World Bank data. Their importance has grown amid volatility in global energy markets following the US-Israel war on Iran, which has sent shockwaves through sectors ranging from agriculture to the garment industry.

In the July-September quarter of the current fiscal year, Saudi Arabia remained Bangladesh’s largest source of remittances. Inflows from the kingdom rose to $1.65 billion, up from $1.23bn in the same period of FY26, according to Bangladesh Bank data.

The kingdom accounted for 19.2pc of Bangladesh’s total remittance inflows in the first quarter of FY27, compared with 16.26pc a year earlier.

During the July-September quarter, overall remittances reached around $8.59bn, with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries continuing to account for the bulk of transfers.

Diversifying overseas jobs is becoming urgent

The latest disruption shows Bangladesh’s heavy reliance on a handful of overseas labour markets, leaving migrant workers and the economy exposed to regional crises.

Since FY2014-15, Saudi Arabia has employed around half of the 9.6 million Bangladeshis who went abroad for work. Workers in the kingdom have sent home an average of $5bn a year.

The pressure on migration is already evident. Overseas employment fell 36pc year-on-year to 134,000 in the July-August period this year, following a decline to around 969,000 workers in FY26, the lowest level in five years, according to Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training data.

Tasneem Siddiqui, executive director of the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU), a local think tank, said the crisis exposed the structural weaknesses of the country’s migration sector.

“Therefore, rather than relying on piecemeal decisions, we must completely overhaul and diversify the manpower market. Otherwise, one crisis after another will emerge, leaving us perpetually vulnerable,” said Tasneem, also a political science professor at Dhaka University.

She said the government needs a long-term strategy to develop skills suited to specific overseas markets and expand employment opportunities beyond traditional destinations.

“Long-term strategic planning is essential. Particularly, allocating a mere 0.08pc of the budget for a $35bn remittance sector is grossly insufficient to accomplish meaningful interventions,” she said.

Meanwhile, economist Zahid said Bangladesh should target countries facing ageing populations and labour shortages, including Japan and countries in eastern Europe, where demand for workers in nursing, caregiving and manufacturing could offer alternatives to Middle Eastern markets.

Sayema Haque Bidisha, an economics professor at Dhaka University, also called for greater diversification of migration destinations, stronger diplomatic engagement and better support for expatriates through overseas missions.

She said Bangladesh needs to improve its international image by demonstrating that its workers can fill skilled jobs, rather than being seen primarily as a source of manual labour.

Shariful Hasan, associate director of BRAC’s Migration Programme and Youth Platform, said earlier this month that many Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia depend on daily or weekly employment and that security concerns have reduced work opportunities.

Pakistan faces greater exposure than India

Bangladesh is not the only country with a significant reliance on remittances from Saudi Arabia.

Its neighbours India and Pakistan also depend on money sent home by their citizens working in the kingdom, although the potential impact varies.

Saudi Arabia is Pakistan’s largest source of remittances, contributing $9.78 billion in the last fiscal year, according to State Bank of Pakistan data.

Meanwhile, around 7pc of India’s international remittance inflows originate from Saudi Arabia. The country receives about $8 billion annually from the kingdom, according to the Reserve Bank of India.

A prolonged crisis that affects employment and earnings in Saudi Arabia could therefore have a greater impact on Pakistan than on India, given Pakistan’s substantial reliance on the kingdom as a source of remittances.

item.description:
In 2019, a group of law students in the Pacific began asking whether governments could be held accountable under international law for their response to climate change. Six years later, in July 2025, the International Court of Justice issued an advisory opinion clarifying states’ climate obligations and responsibilities towards future generations. Young people had helped bring climate change before the world’s highest court.
Yet the money tells a different story. Between 2019 and 2021, youth-led climate justice initiatives received just 0.76% of mitigation-focused funding from some of the world’s largest climate foundations.
The contradiction is stark. Young people can influence international debates and national politics, yet struggle to secure the resources to turn their ideas into action. They are invited to conferences, consulted on policies and celebrated in public campaigns. But how much influence do they have over budgets, institutions and the decisions that determine where climate finance goes?
For Bangladesh, this is more than a question of representation. Generation Z played a defining role in reshaping Dhaka’s political landscape. As the country prepares for COP31, the challenge is to turn that civic influence into lasting institutional change.
Participation must lead to influence
Young people have spent years securing recognition within the UN climate process. YOUNGO, the official constituency for children and youth, gained full status in 2011. COP27 encouraged countries to include youth negotiators in national delegations, while COP28 established the Presidency Youth Climate Champion. At COP30 in Belém, youth consultations engaged thousands of participants.
These are worthwhile steps, but access does not guarantee influence. A conference badge cannot tell us whether young people changed a negotiating position, shaped a policy or influenced a budget. Travel costs, visa restrictions and limited observer places further disadvantage young people from least developed countries, small island developing states and climate-vulnerable communities.
The goal should be to connect participation with decisions, funding and measurable results.
Bangladesh has a foundation on which to build. Its National Adaptation Plan for 2023–2050 provides a long-term framework for climate resilience. Its NDC 3.0, submitted in 2025, includes child-sensitive targets for maintaining essential services during climate shocks. UNICEF has identified it as the first NDC globally to include youth in its measurement, reporting, and verification process.
The International Centre for Climate Change and Development (ICCCAD) at Independent University, Bangladesh, has also demonstrated what practical support can achieve. Between 2023 and 2026, its SIDA-supported CAP-RES project trained 100 youth fellows and funded 57 youth-led climate sub-projects, which together directly reached 47,795 people, nearly half of them women. Such experience shows the value of combining training, mentoring and funding with community-level action.
Still, engagement remains fragmented and often dependent on individual projects and donor support. Opportunities are concentrated in urban centres, while young people from coastal areas, haors, chars and hill districts face greater barriers. Indigenous youth, young women and persons with disabilities need more equitable access. The agenda must also extend beyond adaptation to clean energy, mitigation and green skills, which will shape future employment.
Why climate finance misses young people
The problem is not simply a shortage of money. It is also how funding is designed and distributed.
A review of 100 youth-focused climate finance initiatives by the Commonwealth Secretariat and YOUNGO, launched at COP28, found that funding was generally disbursed in small amounts and information about beneficiaries was often inadequate.
Young applicants may lack established financial systems, organisational experience or evidence of results. Funders, however, also impose complex application requirements and short funding periods that can exclude smaller organisations. Conventional lenders may consider early-stage youth enterprises too risky.
Not every climate initiative should be expected to generate revenue. Community adaptation, disaster preparedness and climate research deliver public benefits that may not produce commercial returns. They need grants and public funding, not debt. Concessional loans, guarantees and blended finance have a role where youth-led enterprises have credible business models and realistic repayment prospects.
International commitments provide an opportunity, but access remains a concern. At COP29, developed countries committed to take the lead in mobilising at least US$300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035, within a broader call to scale climate finance to US$1.3 trillion a year. COP30 called for adaptation finance to increase at least threefold by 2035.
For least developed countries, the terms matter as much as the headline figures. The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, for example, had around US$250 million available for its first call for proposals, against requests estimated at US$2 billion to US$3 billion.
Least developed countries have also committed, through the LDC Initiative for Effective Adaptation and Resilience, to channel 70% of climate finance to local-level action by 2030. Youth-led initiatives should be part of this effort, supported by accessible funding channels and proportionate accountability requirements.
Turning commitments into action
Bangladesh does not need an entirely new climate finance system. It needs to make existing institutions more accessible and accountable.
First, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should formalise youth representation in NDC 3.0 monitoring, National Adaptation Plan reviews, local climate planning and official COP delegations. Selection should be transparent and geographically representative. Institutions should report annually on which youth recommendations were adopted and explain why others were not.
Second, national financing institutions should establish accessible funding windows. Bangladesh Bank could assess how its young entrepreneurs and green finance mechanisms might support viable youth-led climate enterprises. The Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund, Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation and Infrastructure Development Company Limited should create dedicated funding windows or explicitly include eligible youth-led initiatives in existing programmes.
Third, funding must match purpose. Grants should support research, community adaptation, disaster preparedness and early-stage testing. Repayable finance should be reserved for enterprises with credible cash flows. Mentoring, financial-management support and safeguards against excessive debt should accompany funding, with clear pathways for successful pilots to access further grants, public programmes or investment.
Fourth, the Finance Division and environment ministry should introduce a youth marker in annual climate budget reporting. Development partners and national financing institutions should distinguish commitments from actual disbursements. A regularly updated national mapping of youth climate organisations would help identify funding gaps and measure progress.
Fifth, international climate funds should strengthen Enhanced Direct Access, giving accredited National Implementing Entities the resources and authority to establish locally managed youth grant mechanisms. Simplified procedures should be balanced with appropriate technical support and financial oversight.
Finally, Bangladesh and the LDCs Group should use COP31 to press for an adequately resourced Action for Climate Empowerment plan that strengthens young people’s influence over climate decisions. They should also advocate for more accessible finance for locally led climate action and loss and damage, linked to clear national responsibilities and follow-up.
The opportunity in Antalya
Representation without funding leaves young people unable to act. Funding without transparent selection can reinforce existing inequalities. Both require institutions that explain how youth contributions influence decisions and what funded initiatives achieve.
Ahead of COP31 in Antalya this November, Bangladesh has an opportunity to move beyond expressions of support towards measurable commitments: Formal youth representation, accessible financing and transparent reporting. Its experience in climate planning and locally led adaptation gives it a credible basis for making that case.
Generation Z, which helped bring climate change before the world’s highest court in the Pacific and played a defining role in reshaping Dhaka’s political landscape, does not need another pavilion or another invitation to speak. It needs the authority to influence policy, the resources to put ideas into practice, and the means to hold decision-makers accountable.
Giving young people a genuine share of responsibility is not a symbolic gesture. It is a practical investment in those who will live longest with the consequences of decisions made today.
